A unit of data passed between systems, such as "order 42 was placed".

before.note: Read Sharding first: queues often sit between sharded services, and partitioning returns here as the way a log scales. The terms below are enough to begin.

stages.name: Basics
body: When one service calls another directly and waits, a slow or failed callee drags the caller down with it. A message queue breaks that tight coupling: the producer drops a message into the queue and moves on, and a consumer picks it up when it is ready. Amazon describes SQS as a hosted queue that lets you integrate and decouple distributed software systems and components [[sqs-welcome]].

This buys three things. It decouples services, so each can be deployed and scaled on its own. It absorbs bursts: SQS says it can process each buffered request independently, scaling to handle load increases or spikes. And it adds resilience: SQS says it stores messages on multiple servers, so a message waits safely in the queue if a consumer is down rather than being lost [[sqs-welcome]].

There are two broad shapes. A queue hands each message to one consumer, spreading work across a pool, which is good for tasks. Publish-subscribe delivers each message to many subscribers, which is good for broadcasting events. In AMQP, a message is published to an exchange, which distributes message copies to queues using rules called bindings, and the exchange type, such as direct or fanout, decides how [[rabbitmq-amqp]]. Knowing which shape a system needs is the first design choice.

terms.definition: A buffer that holds messages between producers and consumers so they need not run in lockstep.
A sender that puts messages into the queue.
A receiver that takes messages out and processes them.
Letting services run, fail and scale independently by communicating through a queue.
A pattern where each message is delivered to many subscribers, not just one consumer.

stages.name: How it works
body: In the AMQP model a producer does not send straight to a queue. The RabbitMQ page says messages are published to exchanges, which then distribute message copies to queues using rules called bindings; the broker then delivers them to consumers subscribed to the queues [[rabbitmq-amqp]]. This indirection is what lets the same message fan out to many queues without the producer knowing who consumes it.

Delivery needs acknowledgement to be safe. A consumer takes a message, does the work, then acknowledges it. The RabbitMQ page says that if a consumer dies without sending an acknowledgement, the broker redelivers the message to another consumer, or waits for a consumer to register if none is available [[rabbitmq-amqp]]. SQS handles the same problem with a visibility timeout: a received message stays in the queue but is temporarily invisible to other consumers while one works on it [[sqs-visibility]].

Kafka takes a different model built on a log. Its introduction says events are stored durably and reliably for as long as you want, and its design page says a consumer specifies its offset in the log with each fetch request and can rewind it to re-consume data if needed [[kafka-design]] [[kafka-intro]]. Consumers read forward at their own pace, which is closer to a durable record than a disappearing mailbox.

Kafka scales a topic by splitting it into partitions, spread across brokers. The introduction says events with the same event key are written to the same partition, and that Kafka guarantees any consumer of a topic-partition reads that partition's events in exactly the order they were written; it makes no such promise across partitions [[kafka-intro]]. This is the sharding idea you already learned, applied to a message log.

terms.definition: The server that stores messages and delivers them between producers and consumers.
In AMQP, an exchange routes a message to queues according to binding rules.
A consumer's signal that a message was handled, after which the broker can drop it.
A consumer's position in a Kafka log, which it advances as it reads.
One independent, ordered log a Kafka topic is split into, to spread throughput.

stages.name: Going deeper
body: Delivery guarantees are the heart of queue design. Kafka's design page lists them: at most once, where messages may be lost but are never redelivered; at least once, where messages are never lost but may be redelivered; and exactly once, where each message is processed once and only once. It warns that many systems claim exactly-once, so you should read the fine print [[kafka-design]]. Many systems settle on at-least-once and make consumers handle duplicates.

Because at-least-once means a message can arrive twice, consumers must be idempotent: processing the same message twice has the same effect as once. The usual way is to record a message's unique id and skip it if seen before, so a redelivery after a crash does no harm. This is the practical cost of safe delivery. SQS shows the producer side of the same problem: standard queues support at-least-once delivery, and FIFO queues support exactly-once message processing [[sqs-welcome]].

Order and failure handling need explicit decisions. Kafka guarantees order only within a partition, so if two related messages must be processed in order they must share a partition, chosen by a key [[kafka-intro]]. And a message that keeps failing cannot block the queue forever. SQS lets a source queue target a dead-letter queue for messages that are not processed successfully, and a redrive policy's maxReceiveCount sets how many times a consumer can receive a message before it is moved there [[sqs-dlq]].

terms.definition: A message is never lost but may be delivered more than once, so consumers must cope with duplicates.
A consumer where handling the same message twice has the same effect as once.
Whether messages are delivered in order; in Kafka, only within one partition.
The value that decides a message's partition, used to keep related messages ordered together.
A side queue for messages that keep failing, so they do not block the main queue.

stages.name: In practice and trade-offs
body: The two models suit different jobs. A classic broker like RabbitMQ, routing through exchanges with per-message acknowledgement, fits task distribution and complex routing where each message is handled and then gone. A log like Kafka keeps events for as long as you choose, so many consumers, or replays, can read the same ordered history. Many companies run both for different needs.

A queue is powerful but not free. It adds a component to operate and a new failure mode: a backlog. If consumers fall behind producers for long, the queue grows and latency rises. SQS's dead-letter page points to a guide for setting a CloudWatch alarm on messages moved to a dead-letter queue [[sqs-dlq]]. Watching how old the oldest waiting message is, alongside the services themselves, is our suggestion rather than the page's.

Queues also change correctness. Asynchronous processing means a result is not ready the instant a request returns, so the caller must handle "accepted, will finish later". Combined with at-least-once delivery and idempotent consumers, this is the standard way large systems stay decoupled and resilient, and it is why queues come after the data topics they connect.

terms.definition: How far behind the latest message the consumers are; growing lag signals a backlog.
Slowing or buffering producers when consumers cannot keep up, so the system does not fall over.
How long a log keeps messages; after it, old messages age out whether read or not.
Work finishing some time after the request returns, which callers must be designed for.

misconceptions.myth: A queue guarantees each message is processed exactly once.
misconceptions.truth: Kafka's design page lists at-most-once, at-least-once and exactly-once as different guarantees and warns that exactly-once claims often hide fine print; SQS standard queues support at-least-once delivery [[kafka-design]] [[sqs-welcome]].

misconceptions.myth: Messages always come out in the order they went in.
misconceptions.truth: Kafka guarantees order only within a topic-partition; events with the same key go to the same partition [[kafka-intro]].

misconceptions.myth: A producer sends straight to a specific queue.
misconceptions.truth: In AMQP it publishes to an exchange, which distributes copies to queues by bindings [[rabbitmq-amqp]].

misconceptions.myth: Adding a queue removes failure modes.
misconceptions.truth: A message that cannot be processed needs somewhere to go; SQS offers dead-letter queues and points to a guide for alarms on messages moved to one [[sqs-dlq]].
